implementation_notes: Ruby has a real answer to the nonlocal-jump problem — `throw`/`catch`, a tag-based jump that is explicitly for non-exception control flow — so Ruby spaghetti is mostly raised exception types used as breaks and blocks nested deeply enough that the exit path cannot be read. The Ruby-specific tangle is generated code: `define_method`, `method_missing` and DSL-style builders produce control flow that exists only at runtime, which no reader can trace and no static tool can check. `rubocop`'s Metrics/AbcSize and Metrics/CyclomaticComplexity plus Metrics/BlockNesting are the practical gates; `throw`/`catch` should be preferred over exceptions for genuine multi-level exits.
idiom_name: throw/catch used as goto; metaprogramming-generated control flow
code_sketch:
# exception as a break
begin
  rows.each { |r| r.each { |c| raise Found.new(c) if hit(c) } }
rescue Found => f
  f.value
end

# tag-based jump: the right tool in Ruby
value = catch(:found) { rows.each { |r| r.each { |c| throw(:found, c) if hit(c) } }; nil }
pitfalls: `method_missing` makes any method call a runtime dispatch, so a reader cannot enumerate the control-flow edges at all.
`ensure` used as a `finally` with control flow inside it is an implicit goto out of the block.
Blocks that yield and then continue (rather than `return`) change the exit semantics in ways that are invisible at the call site.
